item.title: Contradictory description & implausible test log
item.content:encoded:
Firstly, I noticed in the first paragraph of the description, it says:

The viewing window is opaque to electrons…

However, in the last paragraph of the description it says:

Except for the viewing window, SCP-536 is totally opaque to… subatomic particles.

The latter would indicate that the viewing window is not opaque to electrons.

Secondly, the memo of the second Test Log reads:

It is likely that the Subject's stroke was a result of a combination of mass increase and Lorentz contraction of the blood reaching her brain. Arterial blood was being pushed through the body at close to light speed, and the physical effects of that are probably very unhealthy, even in cases that don't cause immediate death.

I'm fairly certain that if any liquid were to move at close to light speed, it would lacerate and hemorrhage a human target upon impact. In this case it would likely result in an explosive, total rupturing of the subject. If there are intentionally unexplainable interactions caused by the SCP, it was not made clear here.

I love the concept otherwise, it's fascinating and just plain cool.

item.content:encoded:
I'm not thinking time dilation. What I mean by the impaired cognition is that, to someone outside the chamber, you may appear to be moving slower. However, this doesn't translate to impaired mental function for the person inside the chamber.

As for the baseball thing, I mean yeah, it would mess your arm up. Probably, if you could do it. But I think it'd be more than just pain, and as I said, I'm not sure that you'd be able to move that fast anyway. Slow the speed of light, does everything else slow accordingly? In that thrown baseball example, the neural impulses responsible for motor control would travel at superluminal speeds. That's a big no-no as far as physics goes for a number of reasons, not the least of which is that electrons are more massive than photons, unless I'm mistaken.

I think that, from the perspective of someone outside the chamber, everything inside would appear to have slowed, as opposed to now occurring at significant percentages of c. The person inside would, assuming it wasn't outright fatal, feel no difference.

I guess that the effect may be similar to time dilation, even though the person in the chamber is stationary relative to the outside observer's frame of reference. A light clock inside the chamber would, to an outside observer, appear to tick more slowly. To the person inside the chamber, there would be no appreciable difference. Because of this and the other points I've outlined, I do not think the results of exposure to such an environment where c is reduced would be as described. I'm almost certain of this.

Indeed it would. Your heart would effectively have to pump your blood from a stationary position to a significant percentage of "c" with every pump.

Smascher: you're thinking of the classic textbook example of a person who's entire body is moving in a single direction at near the speed of light. That person would observe no ill effects on his or her self.

On the other hand, if your blood is going from 0 to 0.5c with every heartbeat, bad things are likely to happen. Similarly, accelerating your hand (and a baseball) to 0.95c would probably f***k your arm up pretty bad.

I'm also iffy on the described effects here. I'm not sure a person would feel pain due to this. I doubt very much that slowing down the speed of cognition would have the same effects as laughing gas or intoxication, because from the frame of reference of the person that's slowed, there would be no difference. An outside observer would note they appeared to move/think/speak/whatever more slowly, but that doesn't equate to impaired mental function, I don't think.

I think lowering the speed of light significantly could have weird effects on people. Mostly because different parts of the body are all moving at different speeds. Your heart is pumping, blood is moving, your lungs are inflating/deflating. If c is low enough that your blood is moving at 0.95c, while some other part of your body is moving at 0.50c, and you would probably have some strange side effects. Not that they would be the same as what's stated in the text, but weird stuff is plausible I think. Hell, slow it enough that air currents are moving at a significant percentage of the speed of light, and maybe the person would get torn to pieces.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
+ Ok, now that I'm not so tired, actual feedback. Collapsible tab.
- 'Cause it's a lot of feedback.

SCP-536 is to be maintained according to standard Foundation procedures.

This is not containment procedures, this is a cop out to avoid writing them. Things to consider include who can access this, how easy you want it to be to access, and its potential danger.

SCP-536 is a ██ by █ by ██ meter chamber, with a 50 centimeter square viewing window…

You give us the dimensions of the window and a photo of it - it wouldn't be an insurmountable task to extrapolate its dimensions from that. I'd recommend not censoring its dimensions, as I can see no reason why they would be sensitive information.

The viewing window is opaque to electrons, nuclear particles, [REDACTED], and photons of energies above 1 keV.

Except for the viewing window, SCP-536 is totally opaque to electromagnetic radiation and subatomic particles.

These properties are highly anomalous and sure to attract attention, but you simply glaze over them.

I dislike the amount of censorship and the Anti-Foundation links in the recovery log. Why not attribute this to Prometheus Labs? This is right up their alley.

Now, onto the first test. I don't think they would jump into human testing right away… Let me rephrase that. There is absolutely no conceivable circumstance under which they would find a device and have no idea what it does, or know full well what it does for that matter, and immediately throw people inside and begin their dickery with the fundamental forces. Why the hell would they not stick a rock inside? Or a clock? Or a computer running at a predetermined speed? Further, how did the sensors inside the chamber remain operational after being subjected to the same environment that turned the doctor into a black hole? Would the doctor have had enough mass to become a black hole stable for longer than some minuscule fraction of a second?

Second test. Again, unnecessary human testing.

Subsequent analysis of video indicates both Lorentz contraction and redshift of light on the baseball…

Was the baseball thrown at approaching the speed of light, then? If so, where was the observer relative to the baseball's direction of movement? Unless it was thrown away from the observer, I think blueshift is the term you want. I'm also iffy on the described effects here. I'm not sure a person would feel pain due to this. I doubt very much that slowing down the speed of cognition would have the same effects as laughing gas or intoxication, because from the frame of reference of the person that's slowed, there would be no difference. An outside observer would note they appeared to move/think/speak/whatever more slowly, but that doesn't equate to impaired mental function, I don't think.

Third test. Goes without saying. That aside, only issue is:

…approximately zero Carbon-14.

That wording feels odd.

Final test. Again, goes without saying.

1:35:11 Theta dial returned to normal value. Teams in Hazardous Environment suits open the chamber door. Hydrogen gas and high levels of neutron radiation are detected.

Oh boy, an explosion hazard. Good thing the containment procedures… clearly outlined a… ventilation system… to deal… with… No, wait, shit, BOB, DON'T LIGHT A CIG-

My downvote remains pending these issues being addressed. If I'm mistaken anywhere, please correct me.
